title: The Yield Die
primary_metric: net good (yielding) dies per wafer x price per die (revenue per wafer, USD), for each die-size option, computed with every intermediate figure in scientific notation

options.A: The Compact Die -- smaller floorplan, more gross die per wafer, fewer transistors and lower price per chip
options.B: The Full Die -- larger floorplan, fewer gross die per wafer, more transistors and higher price per chip

sources.claim: Standard leading-edge silicon wafer diameter used in current logic manufacturing
sources.title: 200 mm Wafer vs 300 mm Wafer -- A Technical Comparison for Engineers
sources.note: 300mm (12-inch) is the current industry-standard leading-edge wafer diameter, corroborated by WaferWorld's 200/300/450mm comparison.

sources.value: Gross Dies = (Wafer Area / Die Area) - (pi x Wafer Diameter) / sqrt(2 x Die Area)
sources.title: Die Per Wafer Formula & Free Calculators; How Many Chips Per Wafer? GDPW Calculator & Die Yield Guide
sources.note: Two independent industry-technical sources state the same sqrt(2*Area) edge-loss term. AnySilicon's own page also shows a cruder flat 5-10% edge-loss shortcut elsewhere; this case uses the more precise formula, corroborated by siliconanalysts.com's own reference table (omitting their separate 2-3mm edge-exclusion term E for simplicity, a disclosed simplification).

sources.claim: Realistic real-world die-size range used to ground Option A/B's design-choice die areas
sources.value: Small IoT MCU ~25 mm^2; Smartphone SoC ~120 mm^2; Laptop CPU ~200 mm^2; Nvidia H100 ~814 mm^2
sources.title: How Many Chips Per Wafer? GDPW Calculator & Die Yield Guide (2026)
sources.note: Used only to ground Option A (100 mm^2) and Option B (200 mm^2, matching the cited Laptop CPU reference point) as realistic design choices for Priya's fictional chip -- not this case's own chip's confirmed real-world die size.

sources.claim: Transistor density range at TSMC's N3-generation (3nm-class) leading-edge logic node
sources.title: TSMC 3nm Process Packs 250 Million Transistors Per Square Millimeter; TSMC N3, And Challenges Ahead
sources.note: TSMC's own technology-symposium TARGET is 250 MTr/mm^2; independently reported estimates run 167 (high-performance library) to ~290-300 (high-density library) MTr/mm^2. TSMC does not confirm one single exact figure for any specific customer's tape-out -- these are target/estimated figures, used here as the basis for a disclosed representative MA1 value of 200 MTr/mm^2. P6 data-decay check (2026-09-09): the original WikiChip Fuse citation now returns ECONNREFUSED (the site appears to be down/decommissioned, a real dead link, not just bot-blocking) -- swapped to TechPowerUp as the primary url. TechPowerUp itself returned HTTP 403 to an automated fetch (bot-blocking, not confirmed dead -- the figure was directly readable in search-result snippets at the time of research) and a third corroborating outlet (PhoneArena) also 403'd automated fetch. All three independently report the same ~250-300 MTr/mm^2 figure, so the claim is corroborated across three outlets even though none was fully re-fetchable end-to-end on this pass.

sources.claim: Seeds defect-density die-yield model (alpha=1 case of the negative binomial yield model)
sources.as_of: Spring 2014 (course notes; model itself dates to Seeds, 1967)
sources.org: UC Berkeley IEOR (Prof. Robert C. Leachman)
sources.title: Yield Modeling and Analysis -- IEOR 130, Methods of Manufacturing Improvement
sources.note: Directly fetched and confirmed: the notes derive the Poisson model, the Murphy model, and the Seeds model (eq. 10, DY=1/(1+A*D0)) as the alpha=1 case of the general negative binomial yield model. This case uses the Seeds model because it requires no exponential evaluation, matching this case's scientific-notation-only arithmetic target.

sources.claim: Representative defect-density benchmark for a mature, manufacturable leading-edge logic process, and a real corroborating figure (Intel 18A)
sources.value: D0 < 0.1 defects/cm^2 -> ~90% yield for a 1 cm^2 die ("mature, manufacturable" benchmark); Intel 18A reported D0 < 0.40 defects/cm^2
sources.title: How Foundries Calculate Die Yield
sources.note: Directly fetched and confirmed. No foundry discloses its live defect density for a specific tape-out; this is a widely-repeated industry engineering benchmark, not a primary-source measurement, used as the basis for a disclosed representative MA2 value of 0.10 defects/cm^2 (comfortably below Intel's own real disclosed 18A ceiling of 0.40, i.e. representing a more mature line).

sources.title: NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU Architecture (Hopper Architecture Whitepaper)
sources.note: Official, primary-source figure directly from Nvidia's own architecture whitepaper (GH100 die, TSMC 4N/N4-class process). Used only to derive an illustrative dollars-per-transistor benchmark for this case's fictional pricing -- not a claim about this case's own chip.

sources.claim: Real-world street/OEM price range for a packaged Nvidia H100 GPU module
sources.title: NVIDIA H100 Price 2026: $25K-40K, Plus H200/B200/B300
sources.note: Analyst/market estimate, not an official Nvidia list price. This is the price of the fully packaged, sold GPU product (die + HBM memory + board + cooling + Nvidia's own margin), NOT a bare die's price -- used here only as an illustrative real-world anchor to derive a representative dollars-per-transistor rate for this case's fictional chip, disclosed as such (MA3).

sources.claim: Real-world evidence that a larger, more-capable GPU commands a per-transistor price well above a smaller GPU's, not merely a proportional multiple
sources.value: Nvidia L4: 35.8 billion transistors, ~$2,000-$3,000 street price (implied ~7e-8 $/transistor) vs Nvidia H100's ~3.75e-7 $/transistor -- roughly a 5x real gap
sources.title: NVIDIA L4 GPU: Price, Specs & Cloud Pricing Guide
sources.note: Used only to justify the DIRECTION and rough real-world scale of a flagship pricing premium (larger/more-capable chips are priced well above proportional). This case applies a deliberately conservative 19% premium (MA4), a small fraction of the real ~5x gap found between these two specific real products, so the case's dilemma stays genuinely close rather than one-sided.

balance.argument_a: CONFIRMED by case-research (post-P2/P4 remediation, see QA_REPORT.md). The Compact Die wins revenue per wafer at the case's base assumed defect density (D0=0.30, MA2): 492 net good dies x $7,500/die = $3,690,000, versus the Full Die's 191 net good dies x $17,850/die (with the MA4 flagship premium) = $3,409,350 -- an 8.23% margin. At this defect density the Full Die's larger area costs it disproportionately more yield (62.50% vs. 76.92%) than its higher per-die price and premium can offset.
balance.argument_b: The Full Die genuinely wins revenue per wafer at a LOWER defect density: at D0=0.15 (within the -50% sensitivity flex), the Full Die's 235 net good dies x $17,850 = $4,194,750 edges out the Compact Die's 556 x $7,500 = $4,170,000 -- Option B wins by 0.59%. The crossover defect density is approximately D0=0.157-0.16 defects/cm^2: below it, the Full Die's double transistor count and 1.19x flagship pricing premium win; above it (including the case's own base assumption of 0.30), the Compact Die's much larger gross-die-per-wafer count and better-preserved yield win. This is a genuine, real bidirectional dilemma, not a one-sided comparison -- see sensitivity_model.py and QA_REPORT.md's P2/P4 remediation notes.
balance.margin_basis: Revenue per wafer = net good dies (gross dies x Seeds-model yield) x price per die (dollars-per-transistor x transistor count, with a 1.19x flagship premium applied to Option B only per MA4), compared between Option A and Option B. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Transistor density at the assumed leading-edge logic node
modeling_assumptions.basis: A round, representative figure chosen from within the real published range for TSMC's N3-generation logic process (167-300 million transistors/mm^2 across target and independently-reported figures, S4). No foundry confirms one single exact density for a specific customer's tape-out.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales both options' transistor counts and prices by the same factor -- does not change which option wins, only the absolute dollar figures in D5.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Defect density assumed for this tape-out's process node
modeling_assumptions.basis: A representative figure for a leading-edge line that has not yet fully matured -- this is the company's first tape-out on this node, so a higher, less-mature defect density is more defensible than the 'mature, established line' benchmark (D0<0.1, S6), while still sitting below the real, disclosed ceiling (D0<0.40) a major foundry (Intel, 18A) has reported for one of its own newest nodes (S6). This is the one figure in the case not knowable in advance for a specific, not-yet-running process.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: GENUINELY FLIPS THE VERDICT. The Compact Die (Option A) wins at the base case (D0=0.30, 8.23% margin) and at +50% flex (D0=0.45, 15.09% margin, A wins by more). At -50% flex (D0=0.15), the verdict FLIPS: the Full Die (Option B) wins by 0.59%. The crossover is approximately D0=0.157-0.16 defects/cm^2. See sensitivity_model.py and QA_REPORT.md.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Real-world product used to derive the dollars-per-transistor pricing benchmark
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Nvidia H100: 80 billion transistors (S7), $30,000 midpoint of the disclosed $25,000-$40,000 street/OEM price range (S8)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A real, publicly documented AI-chip product used only as an illustrative proxy to derive a per-transistor benchmark -- the H100's price is for a fully packaged, sold GPU module (die + memory + board + cooling), not a bare die, and is not this case's own chip's confirmed market price.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales both options' prices by the same factor -- does not change which option wins, only the absolute dollar figures in D5.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Flagship pricing premium applied to Option B (the Full Die) only, beyond pure linear per-transistor scaling
modeling_assumptions.basis: Real market pricing shows a larger, more-capable chip does not sell for a merely proportional multiple of a smaller chip's price -- comparing two real, disclosed products (Nvidia L4 vs Nvidia H100, S9) shows roughly a 5x real gap in dollars-per-transistor, of which this case applies only a conservative 19% fraction so the dilemma stays genuinely close rather than one-sided.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Works in the OPPOSITE direction from MA2: a higher premium favors Option B, a higher defect density favors Option A. Held fixed while MA2 is flexed for P5; see QA_REPORT.md for the combined finding.

derived.naive_gross_count_ratio_basis: (640 - 306) / 306 * 100 -- the naive, yield-and-price-blind comparison of gross dies alone (Option A's 640 vs Option B's 306), reproduced facilitator-side to quantify exactly how much the naive trap overstates Option A's true revenue-per-wafer edge at the case's base assumption. Never shown to students in case.md.
derived.crossover_basis: The approximate defect density at which Option A and Option B's revenue per wafer are equal, computed by scanning D0 in small increments against the case's own floor-function arithmetic (sensitivity_model.py). Below this value the Full Die (higher price, more transistors) wins; above it the Compact Die (higher yield, more gross dies) wins. The case's base assumption (D0=0.30, MA2) sits above this crossover.

sensitivity_note: The defect density (MA2) is this case's one genuine free scenario dial — no foundry discloses its live defect density, so any figure used is an industry-representative estimate, not a confirmed fact. Unlike the case's first-draft calibration, MA2 now genuinely flips the verdict within the disclosed ±50% sensitivity range (crossover ~D0=0.158, well inside 0.15-0.45). FACILITATOR.md records the sensitivity direction; case.md never states which option wins or by how much.

Four independent fresh-subagent cold-reads were run against this real published artifact, not the case.md fallback: round 1 found 1 gap (unglossed square-root symbol) -> fixed; round 2 found 1 gap (unglossed pi symbol) -> fixed; round 3 found 1 gap (a genuine HTML-entity bug rendering the 10^19 exponent as garbled superscript-n, and three 10^-7 exponents as 10^-5) -> fixed; round 4 found 0 gaps, a clean, unforced PASS. This confirms QA_REPORT.md's own hypothesis that a reader hovering a term inline is a different experience than scanning a 55-row reference table before reading. P7 now records a genuine PASS -- this waiver object is kept for the historical record but no longer governs qa.state.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2 (assumed defect density) is commercially sensitive, undisclosed-by-any-foundry data for a not-yet-running process line -- irreducible unknown at case-authoring time, not knowable in advance by any amount of research (case.json.sensitivity_note; FACILITATOR.md Sensitivity note). P5 finds the verdict GENUINELY FLIPS within the disclosed ±50% flex range: Option A (Compact Die) wins at the base case (D0=0.30, 8.23% margin) and at +50% (D0=0.45, 15.09%), but Option B (Full Die) wins at -50% (D0=0.15, 0.59% margin) -- the real crossover is approximately D0=0.157-0.16. This is a genuine, disclosed bidirectional dependency, not a hidden fragility: D5 already asks every reader to name the one figure their recommendation depends on most and what value would flip it, and this case now has a real, findable answer to that question.
